content: 1. Ideally, the codes used for health facilities should align with those in the national master facility list. This list should specify which HIV services are routinely provided, such as HIV testing services (HTS), antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation, ART dispensing, and CD4 count testing. It should also identify the populations served, especially in cases where facilities cater to specific groups. 2. Monitoring the availability of HIV services can be achieved through routine reporting, evaluations, and special studies. Each country should maintain a national master facility list of all public and private healthcare facilities, which typically requires conducting censuses. 3. The delivery of HIV-specific services in the health sector depends on several components, including service delivery infrastructure, health workforce, medical products and technologies, financing, information systems, and leadership and governance. 4. When updating the national, provincial, or district master health facility list, it is an opportune moment to assess the availability of HIV services. Service readiness is evaluated using both general and specific indicators. 5. General health service readiness indicators include the availability of basic amenities, basic equipment, standard precautions for infection prevention, diagnostic capacity, and essential medicines. HIV-specific service readiness indicators assess the availability of tracer items such as HIV rapid diagnostic tests, antiretroviral drugs, co-trimoxazole, and laboratory tests for CD4 cell counts, early infant diagnosis (EID), and viral load. 6. The presence of healthcare personnel required to provide these services on-site is also assessed. The list of tracer items should align with the expected service delivery at each level of the healthcare system. 7. Service readiness is evaluated by surveying a representative sample of health facilities at national and subnational levels. This assessment should also be integrated into supportive supervision of healthcare personnel. 8. Service availability assessments can identify areas requiring further investment to ensure adequate service delivery and detect specific gaps in equipment, supplies, and staff at individual facilities. Service readiness checklists can also be used for accrediting health services for specific service delivery. 9. To ensure and improve the quality of ART services, national programs, district management offices, and health facilities should have functioning components to support service quality. Indicators in this guide can be used to benchmark service delivery quality for monitoring and guiding quality improvement efforts. 10. At the facility level, below-average performance on these indicators can trigger support for facility-based quality improvement efforts. Facilities should use quality management methods focused on performance measurement data and standardized, routine supportive site supervision. 11. Service quality also includes the acceptability of services and client satisfaction. Exit interviews and hotlines can collect client feedback on waiting times, availability of healthcare providers during clinic hours, convenience of clinic location and hours, and staff attitudes. 12. This feedback can be used for quality improvement efforts at the site level and to help supervisors address issues related to responsiveness to clients’ needs. Indicators for responsiveness have not yet been introduced. 13. Achieving and sustaining the highest attainable level of quality also requires ensuring the appropriate use of biomedical technologies. HIV programs are particularly concerned with clinical laboratory capacity and performance for a range of tests across the prevention, care, and treatment cascade. 14. From a strategic information perspective, laboratories should be reviewed for their capacity, including infrastructure, dedicated laboratory personnel, and equipment, to diagnose HIV infection using rapid tests, enzyme immunoassays (EIA), Western blot, or molecular methods. 15. Laboratories should also be capable of conducting ART monitoring tests, such as viral load and CD4 count, and performing clinical laboratory tests in areas such as hematology, clinical chemistry, serology, microbiology, tuberculosis diagnosis, malaria diagnosis, and diagnosis of opportunistic infections (OIs). 16. Proficiency testing and external quality assurance (EQA) schemes are essential to verify that laboratory standards are met and to implement improvements where needed. 17. Across the HIV care cascade, from diagnosis to retention in care, ART initiation, and viral suppression, service linkages must be monitored to ensure ART programs improve patient health and prevent transmission. However, tools and monitoring systems to assess these linkages are not always user-friendly. 18. Evaluations should be conducted to assess service linkages and guide the implementation of systems to track clients through these linkages. The integration of ART with other services, such as tuberculosis, maternal and child health, and community-based services, should also be emphasized in monitoring and evaluation strategies. 19. Monitoring should include ART initiation in these programs and the linkage of eligible patients to continuing ART services. Service linkage does not occur in isolation; clear responsibilities must be assigned, and referral pathways must be identified in standard operating procedures (SOPs). 20. Information on the health workforce is essential for planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating health sector programs and strategies. Understanding the dynamics of the health workforce helps identify opportunities and limitations for scaling up interventions. 21. The size and distribution of the health workforce depend on the inflow and outflow of workers into the labor force, as well as their movement between sectors, geographic locations, and countries. To assess human resource capacity for delivering essential health services, basic information such as coverage, graduation rates in health professions, and vacancy rates must be monitored. 22. For HIV programs, disaggregating these measurements by cadre of healthcare workers, region, specialization, and place of work (urban/rural and facility type) provides a more detailed picture of human resource capacity for specific HIV-related needs. 23. It is important to assess not only the number of healthcare workers in HIV services but also whether their geographic distribution matches the epidemic's pattern (e.g., hotspots, urban/rural, regional) and whether the needs of specific priority populations are being met. 24. Effective HIV programs rely on the continuous availability of essential drugs and supplies. Tracking key aspects of the procurement and supply management system can identify gaps and bottlenecks, enabling corrective actions to avoid stock-outs and over-stocks. 25. WHO has developed tools to measure key aspects of the pharmaceutical sector and systematically monitor progress in improving access to essential medicines. These tools can assess the integrity of the supply of medicines and health products in HIV programs. 26. For assessing the drug and procurement system for HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria programs, WHO and partners have developed a set of 12 core indicators. These indicators use routinely collected data to monitor and evaluate critical components of the supply chain. 27. These indicators are relevant for all national procurement and supply management systems, donors, and institutions. Monitoring the availability, reliability, and completeness of information for these core indicators can assess how well the information system functions and whether it generates the essential information required to inform policy and planning for the health sector response to HIV. 28. Policies, regulations, and laws influence every step of the continuum of prevention, care, treatment, and support. They are critical structural factors that can determine the success or failure of responses to the HIV epidemic. 29. Monitoring and evaluating the outcomes and impacts of ART must consider policies and laws to verify whether they align with best public health practices, are known to service providers and affected communities, and are implemented effectively. 30. Policies and laws that positively influence ART access, use, and retention (e.g., mandating gender-sensitive, equitable access to quality ART, promoting non-discrimination, and protecting privacy) should be documented, as well as those with negative impacts that drive key populations underground by criminalizing their behaviors. 31. UNAIDS and partners have developed a National Commitments and Policies Instrument (NCPI) to measure progress in developing and implementing national HIV policies, strategies, and laws. This instrument is complemented by a set of policy and practice questions developed by WHO. 32. Both sets of questions are included in the Global AIDS Response Progress Reporting (GARPR) and should be reviewed and reported regularly (annually or biennially).
